one_liner: Original coverage-guided fuzzer: edge-coverage feedback plus a fork server; far more code reached than blind mutation fuzzing.
what_it_does: afl-fuzz mutates a queue of input files, runs an instrumented target on each one (on stdin or via an @@ file argument) and keeps any input that produces new edge coverage, so it finds crashes and hangs deep in parsers that random mutation never reaches. Targets are rebuilt with drop-in compiler wrappers (afl-gcc/afl-g++, afl-clang, or afl-clang-fast from llvm_mode), or run unmodified under a patched QEMU in user-emulation mode. Companion tools afl-tmin, afl-cmin, afl-showmap and afl-analyze minimise inputs and corpora and inspect coverage. It is a command-line tool, not a library: you write a small harness that reads a file and calls your code.
how_it_is_fast: Compile-time instrumentation adds shared_mem[cur ^ prev]++ at every branch, with random block ids, into a 64 kB shared-memory bitmap that fits in L2 and is compared with the global map in a few word-wide operations; hit counts are bucketed (1, 2, 3, 4-7, ... 128+) so loop-count changes register as new behaviour. A fork server stops the target at its first instrumented function and clones it with copy-on-write fork() instead of execve() per input (docs: usually 1.5-2x on fast targets); deferred __AFL_INIT() skips user initialisation (10x+ on some targets) and persistent __AFL_LOOP() reuses one process for many inputs (5x or more). Search effort is kept cheap with test-case trimming, periodic corpus culling that favours small, fast entries, and aggressive timeouts (5x the calibrated run time, rounded up to 20 ms).
when_to_use: Fuzzing C or C++ file-format parsers, decoders and libraries whose source you can rebuild with afl-gcc or afl-clang-fast, ideally with a small harness that reads one file from stdin or @@.

Pairing with AddressSanitizer (AFL_USE_ASAN) or AFL_HARDEN and libdislocator to turn silent memory corruption into crashes the fuzzer can see, within the memory-limit constraints in notes_for_asan.txt.
Black-box Linux binaries with no source via QEMU mode, accepting the documented 2-5x slowdown against compile-time instrumentation.
Building a small, self-contained corpus of 'does something new' inputs to seed slower test regimes (browsers, office suites, closed-source tools), as the README suggests.
Learning how coverage-guided fuzzing works: docs/technical_details.txt explains every design choice in plain text.
when_not_to_use: New fuzzing campaigns: the repository was archived on 2024-03-22 and the last release is 2.57b (2020-06-30); AFL++ (release 5.03c) is the maintained fork and calls itself faster with more and better mutations, but its default licence is now AGPL-3.0-or-later (harness-compiled parts stay Apache-2.0).
Recent clang/LLVM: llvm_mode is reported broken with LLVM/Clang 13 (open issues #151 and #156), and persistent and deferred modes only work with afl-clang-fast.
Fast, stateless library APIs where exec rate is everything: llvm_mode/README.llvm itself says persistent mode is not as fast as in-process fuzzing such as LLVM's libFuzzer.
Network services, daemons, interactive programs, or formats wrapped in checksums, signatures, encryption or compression: no direct support, and coverage stays shallow unless you patch the checks out.
Very large targets: the fixed 64 kB map collides on about 7% of tuples at 10,000 branches, 14% at 20,000 (sqlite) and 30% at 50,000.

integration.form: built tool (make): afl-fuzz plus compiler wrappers and a runtime object linked into the instrumented target
integration.dependencies: none for the core (GNU make and a C compiler); llvm_mode needs clang with llvm-config and LLVM development headers; qemu_mode builds a patched QEMU
integration.min_toolchain: GCC or clang for afl-gcc/afl-clang; llvm_mode reported failing with LLVM/Clang 13 (#151, #156); built with -O3 -funroll-loops by default
integration.platforms: Linux x86 (primary); OpenBSD, FreeBSD and NetBSD on x86 with gmake; macOS on x86 with caveats (slower fork(), crash reporter must be disabled); Solaris reportedly; non-x86 via AFL_NO_X86=1 with llvm_mode or QEMU; QEMU mode Linux only; Android support added in 2.57b
integration.thread_safety: afl-fuzz runs one target process at a time per instance; scale with parallel -M/-S instances that sync queues. In targets, afl-gcc/afl-clang keep the previous-location state in a global and afl-clang-fast in a thread-local variable; bitmap counter updates are not atomic, so multi-threaded targets give noisier coverage.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces a blind mutation fuzzer for any target that reads a file or stdin, but the target must be rebuilt with AFL's compiler wrappers (or run under the slower QEMU mode), and persistent or deferred speed-ups need source changes

gotchas: Evidence check: the coverage tables come from one afl-fuzz session on GNU patch 2.7.3, with no CPU, run count or variance, and the docs do not say how blocks and edges were counted; 'Blind fuzzing L' was given a comparable number of execution cycles, while the guided runs needed more time, so the strategies were not compared at equal wall time. All baselines are AFL itself with guidance removed. The speed ratios (fork server 1.5-2x, persistent 5x or more and 5-10x in perf_tips.txt, deferred 10x+, llvm_mode up to 2x) are prose against AFL's own slower modes, not measurements against another fuzzer.

64-bit ASAN builds reserve huge virtual memory and clash with the default 50 MB child memory limit (-m); notes_for_asan.txt recommends 32-bit builds, cgroups limits or careful measurement, and ASAN cannot be combined with -static.

Persistent and deferred modes must fully reset target state and must start before threads, timers, sockets or any access to the input; otherwise you get false positives or wasted cycles. Targets that install their own SIGSEGV/SIGABRT handlers hide crashes from afl-fuzz.
AFL produces no human-readable coverage report (the README points to afl-cov), and edge hit counters can wrap to zero because the instrumentation has no saturating add.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings is a fuzzer; AFL is the coverage engine they serve. RetroWrite and E9Patch are static binary rewriters that can add AFL-style coverage to binary-only targets, and are worth trying before AFL's QEMU mode with its 2-5x cost; AddressSanitizer is the usual bug detector to compile into an AFL target.
verified_claims_summary: AFL's own technical notes report a single pass over the queue on GNU patch 2.7.3 (-O3, dummy text seed): the AFL model reached 1,765 blocks and 2,597 edges against 182/205 (blind, one round), 228/265 (blind, comparable cycles), 855/1,130 (block-coverage guidance) and 1,452/2,070 (edge-coverage guidance), and with deterministic stages only from a valid diff 1,452/2,040 and 1 crash against 1,101/1,409 blind with no crashes. CPU, compiler for the instrumented build, run count and the blind and block-guided harness variants are not published.
status_note: Abandoned: last release 2.57b (2020-06-30), last commit 2021-06-08, archived 2024-03-22; Apache-2.0 and easy to build, but new campaigns should start from the maintained AFL++ fork.
